speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF DISTINGUISHED VISITORS FROM NIGERIA AND AUSTRALIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
it is a great privilege today to be able to welcome to the house distinguished representatives from Nigeria. We have in Your Honour's gallery Alhaji Sir Ahmadu Bello, Sardauna of Sokoto, premier of the northern region, and also Alhaji Sir Muhammadu Sanusi, Emir of Kano who has over 3 million subjects in his emirate. In addition there are three distinguished ministers from the northern region of Nigeria, Hon. Alhaji Isa Kaita, Minister of Education, Hon. Malam Ibrahim Musa Gashash, Minister of Lands and Surveys and Hon. G. U. Ohikere, Minister of Works.
As hon. members know, the northern region of Nigeria contains well over half the population of that country and has over half the members in the federal parliament. We are delighted to have these distinguished public servants with us in Canada and also to have the opportunity of conferring with them on various subjects which are of interest to both our countries.
On October 1 Nigeria will gain its independence, and all Canadians look forward to the time when Nigeria will be one of our sister nations of the commonwealth. We firmly believe that this new nation has a vital part to play in the commonwealth and also in the continent of Africa, the United Nations and the councils of the world. We are very happy that there exists today between Nigeria and Canada the closest ties of friendship. With those thoughts we welcome these visitors to our gallery this morning.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF DISTINGUISHED VISITORS FROM NIGERIA AND AUSTRALIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we on this side are glad to have the opportunity of sharing in the welcome which has been expressed in such fitting terms by the Secretary of State for External Affairs to our distinguished visitors from Nigeria, gentlemen who have served their people well in the past and who
will have even greater opportunities for service in the future. We welcome them not only because of their personal distinction but also because they represent a country which as the minister has pointed out is on the threshold of independence, an independence which we hope will also mean association as a free state in our commonwealth of nations.
Hon. members of this house without exception, I am sure, will support any Canadian government in any move it may make to assist this new nation of the commonwealth with the fourth largest population in the commonwealth and in any move that may be made to bring us closer together. Though far away geographically and differing in the circumstances of its background, we in Canada are anxious to work with the people of Nigeria in the promotion of all good causes; for freedom, democracy and peace in the world.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF DISTINGUISHED VISITORS FROM NIGERIA AND AUSTRALIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the members of this group join with the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the leader of the official opposition in their welcome to the premier of Northern Nigeria and his colleagues and in the comments they made during their brief remarks. We in this group rejoice in this demonstration of the spirit of brotherhood that can be found and promoted within the commonwealth. We salute and welcome these representatives of another country soon to take its place within the ranks of the nations within the commonwealth. We trust, Mr. Speaker, that as a result of their visit to Ottawa and discussions with representatives of the government on matters about which they must be seriously concerned, such as technical assistance and relations within the commonwealth, they will find their visit most fruitful and enjoyable and, when they return to Nigeria, in the days ahead will be able to look back on their visit to Ottawa and say in the words of the poet Moore:
When time, which steals our years away,
Shall steal our pleasures, too,
The memory of the past will stay,
And half our joys renew.

speakeroldname: Mr. Richard A. Bell (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: ORGANIZATION FOR ECONOMIC CO-OPERATION AND DEVELOPMENT-REPORT ON PARIS MEETINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Minister of Finance is engaged this morning at the dominion-provincial conference, he has asked me to report to the house on his behalf on the meetings held in Paris on July 22 and July 23 to consider the proposed establishment of a new organization for economic co-operation and development to replace the existing organization for European economic co-operation.
Hon. members will recall that on January 18 the Minister of Finance informed the house of the results of the first organizational meeting which had arisen from the initiative taken at the end of last year by the United States, the United Kingdom, France and Germany. From that meeting a number of important proposals emerged designed to strengthen and facilitate economic co-operation amongst the countries of western Europe, the United States and Canada. One of the most important was that the existing O.E.E.C. should be reconstituted to meet the problems and challenges of the 1960's. In the new O.E.C.D. Canada and the United States would become full members together with the 18 western European governments now members of the O.E.E.C. and representatives of the European communities.
In Paris last week ministerial representatives made substantial progress toward these ends and agreed upon the broad lines of a (Mr. Speaker.]

convention for the organization. Over the next few months remaining details concerning the convention and the scope of its activities will be worked out. It is anticipated that by the end of the year member governments will be in a position to sign a convention which would be submitted to their respective legislatures for approval. We have indicated our intention to sign this convention, and if this timetable is realized the government will, at an appropriate stage, submit to the house for approval the charter of the new organization.
The meeting also appointed Mr. Kristensen of Denmark as secretary general designate of the new organization. Mr. Kristensen is a former finance minister of his country and brings to this very important post a distinguished political and administrative background. His first task will be as chairman of the preparatory committee which was established to work out the remaining details prior to signature.
The new organization will, it is expected, have three main functions. It will provide a forum for consultation about economic policies of member governments. Progress made in liberalization of trade and payments and the introduction of convertibility in Europe have led to a closer interdependence of the economies of member countries, which makes consultation necessary and desirable.
The organization will also have an important role to play in stimulating and coordinating more closely the efforts of the more advanced countries to assist the less developed countries of the world. This would in no way limit or change the nature of our existing aid programs such as the Colombo plan, nor would it involve a direct obligation on the part of Canada to provide additional assistance. However, most of the important aid-giving countries are members of the new organization, and it is the hope of the Canadian government that there will be a useful role for the organization to play in the aid field by way of exchange of information and experience.
Finally it was agreed that the new organization, in conformity with its objectives, should seek to promote the expansion of trade on a multilateral, non-discriminatory basis. The 20 countries were all agreed that any trade activities of the new organization should be fully in accordance with the obligations of member countries to GATT and the international monetary fund, and it was urged that these activities should contribute to the attainment of the objectives of these broader international organizations.
As the house knows, this is a point to which we in Canada attach the highest importance. Over 30 per cent of our trade is

done with the European countries of the proposed O.E.C.D. At the same time, like other exporting nations within that group, we attach great importance to our trade with the rest of the world. Thus in these meetings, with delegations from other like-minded nations, the Canadian delegation emphasized that it should be the purpose of this organization to encourage the expansion of mutually profitable trade throughout the world. I am pleased to report that the deliberations were, in fact, guided by this spirit and there existed a genuine desire to work together for the achievement of this important objective.
The Minister of Finance has asked me to make it clear to the house that no direct attempt was made at this meeting to settle the specific problems between the common market Six and the free trade association of the Seven. Canada is confident, however, that the O.E.C.D. will help to establish a climate in which these and other economic issues can be resolved in a manner consistent with our world-wide trade objectives and interests. While the O.E.C.D. will not constitute an exclusive or inward-looking economic bloc in any sense, Canada hopes that it will help to further a harmonious spirit of co-operation among the countries of western Europe and Canada and the United States, and in this way strengthen the free world.
With the permission of the house, Mr. Speaker, I should like now to table a copy of the resolution adopted at the conclusion of the Paris meeting last Saturday evening. It may be the wish of the house to have this resolution printed as an appendix to today's Hansard.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: ORGANIZATION FOR ECONOMIC CO-OPERATION AND DEVELOPMENT-REPORT ON PARIS MEETINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think members of the house will have listened with very great interest to the report which the parliamentary secretary, due to the understandable absence of the Minister of Finance this morning, has made on the meeting recently concluded in Paris, a meeting which is of very great significance and importance to all member states involved and to no state more than to Canada. It was a meeting which looked toward the transformation of the organization for European economic co-operation, which has played such a constructive part in economic development in Europe in past years, into the organization for economic co-operation and development, which we hope will extend the scope of the earlier organization across the Atlantic, and in which the United States and Canada will be able to play a full and important part.
The parliamentary secretary gave us some information about the meeting, but I should
79951-0-434
Paris Trade Meetings
like to point out that Saturday's London Times, which I was able to read this morning, contains an even more detailed report which has the ring at least of authority. This report refers to a resolution submitted to the conference by the United States delegate, Mr. Dillon, suggesting powers to be accorded to the trade committee of this new organization, powers which apparently are to be rather extensive in this field and will have a relationship to GATT itself. This London Times report goes on to say that the United States draft resolution on the future functions of the trade committee of O.E.C.D. foresees a confrontation of general trade policies, an examination of specific trade differences of member countries, and consideration of any remaining short or long term problems not solved by the existing trade committee of 21 powers. This is an indication, Mr. Speaker, of the far-reaching functions which are to be proposed, at least by the United States, for this new body.
It would be interesting to learn the attitude of the Canadian minister and the Canadian delegation to this specific United States proposal. In any event, Mr. Speaker, the move in Paris is an important one; it is a constructive one, and I hope the organization will be, in the words of the parliamentary secretary, an outward-looking body. In this respect it will certainly receive the wholehearted support of the members on this side.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION FOR ECONOMIC CO-OPERATION AND DEVELOPMENT-REPORT ON PARIS MEETINGS
speechtext:
There has recently arisen, Mr. Speaker, quite a lot of concern at the impending action on the part of the inner six of Europe, as a result of the proposal to raise tariff barriers on imports into their trading region. There is growing fear also that the inner six and the outer seven, rather than moving closer together are moving farther apart, and accompanying this is the realization that unless we have very early action, the economic unity which existed in the western world may be greatly endangered.
We, of course, naturally welcome the move that is now being made. However, unlike the Leader of the Opposition, I read into the announcement no far-reaching functions of the new organization, and I have particular reference to the lack of any indication that one of the main functions of this organization is to enhance the economic unity of the Atlantic world.
I took it to be a welcome announcement that there would be extensive consultation. However, in my opinion there was a lack in the announcement of the specific responsibility that was planned for this new organization. I must admit that a complicated statement

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO SENDING OF CANADIAN FORCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether it is a fact, as reported, that the United Nations have asked Canada for 100 signallers for the United Nations Congo force but that 25 only have been supplied to date.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO SENDING OF CANADIAN FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on July 22 I informed the house that discussions with the secretary general were going on concerning an inquiry as to whether Canada could provide signals specialists for the force. I point out that these are not ordinary signallers. The secretary general has also inquired whether we would be in a position to provide assistance for parts of the logistics support of the force.
Since receiving those inquiries the government has been engaged in detailed discussions with the secretariat with a view to clarifying the needs of the United Nations. The matter had to be studied in the light of requirements of the force as assessed by its commander, and appropriate Canadian army officers have been in touch with Major General Alexander in New York, since he was widely experienced in the actual conditions in the Congo. As hon. members will recall, Major General Alexander went to the Congo in command of the forces from Ghana. No precise figures have emerged from these discussions as yet, but the Canadian army has been considering tentative establishments, including a signals squadron of about 100 all ranks. This also involves complicated questions of equipment, and there have been discussions on that point as well.
One difficulty arises because any Canadian army personnel involved would have to be immunized against the tropical diseases so prevalent in the area before they could be

sent to the Congo. This process of immunization has been started for a number of selected personnel. There has also been discussion about sending some of the Canadian signals specialists from the United Nations emergency force in Palestine to the Congo, and that, I presume, is where this mention of 25 originated. It is not clear yet whether they could be spared from the United Nations emergency force, but that particular aspect of the question is also under discussion at the present time.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO SENDING OF CANADIAN FORCES
speechtext: Could I ask a supplementary question. In the light of what the minister has said, will he comment on the report that the Canadian government plans to send between 300 and 800 administrative, non-combat troops to the United Nations force in the Congo, and would these signallers be included in that contingent mentioned in this report?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO SENDING OF CANADIAN FORCES
speechtext: That report is of course purely speculative, and when there is an announcement to make about the troops to be sent it will be made in the house. I would presume that the signals specialists are meant to be included in that report.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Minister of Transport. Has the minister any information which he can give to this house about the fatal train accident which occurred in Montreal last Saturday?

subtopic: MONTREAL, QUE.  REPORT ON FATAL ACCIDENT
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, I have here a report from the board of transport commissioners dealing with this matter.
In accordance with standing instructions, the board's district inspector at Montreal has made a preliminary review of the circumstances surrounding this accident and his report is now on file. Full information with respect to the circumstances contributing to this accident will not be available until completion of the investigation, but the following information may be of some help.

that a person who is speaking on a question of privilege should not be interrupted by anyone else on a point of order. Having now been given an opportunity to make that explanation, I do not hesitate to withdraw the word "unfair".

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MR. DESCHATELETS-REFERENCE TO PROCEEDINGS IN HUMAN RIGHTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The
point I was endeavouring to make was a point of order with respect to this whole question of whether a matter which took place in a committee can be raised as a question of privilege in this way.

subtopic: MR. DESCHATELETS-REFERENCE TO PROCEEDINGS IN HUMAN RIGHTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: How do you know that the matter was?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MR. DESCHATELETS-REFERENCE TO PROCEEDINGS IN HUMAN RIGHTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Surely it is desirable, before we decide whether it is proper to raise the question of privilege, to address our attention to the question of whether the rules provide for its being done in this way. That was the reason I rose on a point of order. I did so because I felt it was essential that the house should determine that matter. I did not interrupt any hon. member. I rose on a point of order, and I was given the floor by Mr. Speaker for the purpose I have just outlined. That is, of course, a perfectly proper procedure.
My point of order is that it is my recollection of the rules of the house that matters taking place in a committee cannot be referred to until the committee has reported. That is the first, general rule. Second, if any member of a committee does desire to question the proceedings of that committee he must do so by way of a report from the committee; there must be a reference from the committee to the Speaker, as I recall it, in a formal way by way of an appeal from the ruling of the Chair, or something of that nature, or by way of a report from the chairman raising for the consideration of the house the matter which is complained of in the committee. Neither of these things has happened. The committee has not reported generally, nor has a specific matter been reported by the chairman of the committee to the house. Neither has the member-and I am not sure that in any case the rules provide for this-appealed to this house from a ruling of the chairman, or anything of that nature.
I submit, therefore, that it is improper for any hon. member to seek to raise a matter of the kind which the hon. member is seeking to raise as a question of privilege, at least until the committee has reported. It is quite obvious what the hon. member is seeking to do, and I submit to Your Honour that this is clearly a case where the rules of the house regarding privilege should not be allowed to be abused in order that a member
Inquiries of the Ministry may make a statement in the house, in the guise of a question of privilege, which is completely out of order.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MR. DESCHATELETS-REFERENCE TO PROCEEDINGS IN HUMAN RIGHTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: I should like to ask you two questions, Mr. Speaker, in respect of this point of order. Can there be any interruption of a statement on a question of privilege by anyone in this house except Your Honour? The second is, how can the minister raise a point of order about a question of procedure until the statement of the member raising that question of privilege has been completed?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. DESCHATELETS-REFERENCE TO PROCEEDINGS IN HUMAN RIGHTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Perhaps that matter can be dealt with. We are really getting involved in two points of order at the same time. As to the question asked by the Leader of the Opposition about the raising of a point of order while a question of privilege is being discussed, my understanding of the procedure is that that is quite permissible. However, a second point of order cannot be raised while the first point of order is under discussion.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MR. DESCHATELETS-REFERENCE TO PROCEEDINGS IN HUMAN RIGHTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
May I point out that the hon. member in rising on a question of privilege stated that it had to do with a vote which had taken place in a committee of this house. That fact is before us, and once that had been stated I submit that the Minister of Justice was quite correct in raising his point of order.
The rules of the house normally prevent any question of privilege being raised in respect of votes taken in committees. If that were not the case the business of this house could be interrupted time and again by any individual member of a committee who did not happen to like the way members of the committee had voted. He could come into this house and raise a question of privilege, arguing that a vote had been taken on such and such a question and that it should not have been taken. It is fundamental in our parliamentary procedure that the committee controls its own work. As I understand it, there is not even provision for appeal from the decisions made by the chairman of a committee. I suggest that the hon. member who raised this question of privilege is completely out of order.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. DESCHATELETS-REFERENCE TO PROCEEDINGS IN HUMAN RIGHTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: May I be allowed to speak to the point of order?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. DESCHATELETS-REFERENCE TO PROCEEDINGS IN HUMAN RIGHTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I will be glad to hear the hon. member on the point of order and when it is resolved then, of course, the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont will have the floor again in the light of the decision as to what may be properly raised.

Inquiries of the Ministry

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. DESCHATELETS-REFERENCE TO PROCEEDINGS IN HUMAN RIGHTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The point of order I should like to bring to Your Honour's attention is this. There was an attempt to raise in this house a matter of privilege dealing with something that happened elsewhere but still within the precincts of this house. While that was under discussion it was impossible for the house to know what it was all about; certainly for me to know what it was all about, because I am not a member of the committee. Three hon. members have risen on a point of order and even yet the house knows nothing about the matter raised under privilege.
While perhaps the points of order were taken in the light of the rules, still I think the house should know and is entitled to know what it is that the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont has in mind so that Your Honour under the circumstances may make a decision. That is my submission to you, sir.

subtopic: MR. DESCHATELETS-REFERENCE TO PROCEEDINGS IN HUMAN RIGHTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I say a word on the principle involved. I think it is a well-understood rule and practice and an established guarantee of our rights that an hon. member can raise a question of privilege. This supersedes any other order of business or anything before the house. It is in order for an hon. member to raise a question of privilege at any time. If we say that a point of order supersedes a question of privilege, then there is no question of privilege available to hon. members. The right of a member of parliament to raise a question of privilege at any time and to state it briefly without interruption is one of our fundamental rights.
I would ask Your Honour to consider this and not be led into the error of saying that an hon. member who has initiated a question of privilege can be interrupted by someone else who raises a point of order. In my opinion, in the circumstances, a question of privilege supersedes any so-called point of order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. DESCHATELETS-REFERENCE TO PROCEEDINGS IN HUMAN RIGHTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I wish to thank hon. members who have contributed to the consideration of this problem. If I may give my view in the light of what has been said, it is this; the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont rose on a question of privilege, quite properly, but began to discuss a proceeding which occurred in a committee this morning until he had proceeded far enough that I had doubts that he would be in order in accordance with our practice, which does not permit the review of committee proceedings in this house except after report. I asked him then to justify the regularity of his course. Perhaps I intervened too soon. I wanted to be sure I was on sound ground in ruling, as I shall have to do, that the house


does not review the decisions of the chairman of a committee or the proceedings in a committee, nor does it hear about them until they have been reported.
In the light of the discussion, if the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont feels that the privileges of the house are involved in some way I should like him to state his question of privilege, having in mind that we are not here to hear appeals from or to review the conduct of the committees.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Justice. speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTED OSTRACIZING OF CHINESE FAMILIES IN MONTREAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have seen the report in the Montreal Gazette to which the hon. member refers. Once again a report appears in the newspapers containing allegations of misconduct on the part of the police without there being any chance, as the report is worded, of our investigating it to see whether or not the facts as alleged are correct.
In the light of these circumstances, therefore, I have to repeat to the house what I said before in answer to similar questions. On every occasion when an incident has been brought to our attention or an allegation has been made, in a manner which did give us

any possibility of investigating it as an identifiable incident, we have investigated it most thoroughly and promptly, and in each such case it has been established that the allegation of misconduct on the part of the police was not true with one exception to which I think I should refer again, the case in Prince Rupert where Chinese were asked to sign questionnaires which they should not have been asked to sign. I think that was in six instances only.
I have made statements before as to the role of the Hong Kong police in this inquiry. I have taken every necessary step to satisfy myself-and I am convinced that every hon. member would be satisfied-that the Hong Kong police are conducting themselves properly, that they are acting as interpreters only in their contacts with individuals being questioned, that they are not abusing anybody or attempting to use intimidation or uttering threats. They are there with the Chinese only in the presence of our R.C.M.P. officials. The questions are asked by the R.C.M.P. and then interpreted by the Hong Kong police. Certainly the allegation contained in the Gazette in this form is an example of the kind of vague insinuation that it is impossible to deal with. This is what is said:
We have been told, however, that among the Chinese questioned here, twelve have been made to sign documents of some sort or other by the Hong Kong officers.
Now, sir, could there be anything more nebulous by way of vague insinuation, without an iota of identification, whether of the persons involved, or of the documents that are being talked about, or of the time and place of the incidents?
I think I should inform the house that it appears, with respect to those who have been involved in this racket, that there is a deliberate attempt to force, by intimidation, the other members of the Chinese community to refuse to co-operate with the police. This sort of allegation of improper police methods is in my view a part of that campaign. All I can say further about it is that if anyone brings to my attention an incident which I can investigate, then an investigation will be made immediately and thoroughly. I have investigated all incidents that have come to my attention thus far and have found the allegations to be unfounded. I therefore answer the hon. member's question by saying that my discussion with the police again this morning on the basis of this report, unidentified as I say, has further convinced me that there is no foundation for allegations of this type.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REPORTED OSTRACIZING OF CHINESE FAMILIES IN MONTREAL
speechtext:
A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Why is it that Canadian-born Chinese are not being used as interpreters rather than the Hong Kong police?
Inquiries of the Ministry

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTED OSTRACIZING OF CHINESE FAMILIES IN MONTREAL
speechtext: One very good reason is that this investigation covers activities in Hong Kong. The knowledge of the Hong Kong police as to the situation there is essential. It is essential that we have someone with a knowledge of the situation there as well as with a knowledge of the Chinese language.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REPORTED OSTRACIZING OF CHINESE FAMILIES IN MONTREAL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, another supplementary question. Is this not a question of translation; and if it is a question of translation and/or interpretation, then surely there must be Canadian-born Chinese who are able to translate just as competently as the Hong Kong police.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTED OSTRACIZING OF CHINESE FAMILIES IN MONTREAL
speechtext:
I have endeavoured to explain that the Hong Kong police have discharged other roles and are assisting us in other matters than that of mere translation. In connection with their contact with witnesses, their role and their relation to the witnesses are confined to the translation of questions and answers. However, they are helping us in this inquiry in many other ways besides the interpretive role.
This is a matter of police operation. I have confidence in the officials who are carrying out the operation, but notwithstanding that confidence, as I have said, every case where an allegation is made that we can identify we have investigated fully, promptly and thoroughly, with the result I have indicated to the house, that these allegations are unfounded and appear to be a campaign on the part of those involved in the racket to persuade the rest of the Chinese community not to co-operate with the police in the investigation.
That could have only one result, namely that the racket would go unexposed and the Chinese community would continue in the unfortunate situation in which it finds itself now, namely the victim of an organized racket which we are endeavouring to expose and stamp out.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: REPORTED OSTRACIZING OF CHINESE FAMILIES IN MONTREAL

subtopic: REPORTED OSTRACIZING OF CHINESE FAMILIES IN MONTREAL
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, I have indicated that the Hong Kong police have our confidence and that they are behaving themselves in a proper manner.

On clause 1-Article.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this bill has now been reported back to the house by the banking and commerce committee, which held 24 meetings and heard at least 39 representations.
With respect to amendments, the government indicated its readiness to accept amendments which would improve the bill and four such amendments were made in the committee. Two other amendments were moved which were not accepted. With respect to one of them particularly, the one dealing with the position of industry engaged in export business, I gave an undertaking to the committee to reconsider the matter very carefully to see whether an amendment could safely be included in the bill. I expect to be in a position to report to the committee on that matter either later today or on another occasion when we are dealing with the bill.
I should like to conclude this portion of my remarks simply by saying that the committee gave the bill admirable and thorough study. It was assisted greatly by a wide variety of representations that were made, and the study of the committee confirms my impression that this is a good bill; that it clarifies the combines legislation; that in some respects it does this in a way that will be of assistance to industry in enabling them without fear of prosecution to carry out activities which will be beneficial to the economy and which we were advised previously they refrained from carrying out because of the uncertainty of the legislation.
I therefore wish to express appreciation of the consideration of this matter by the committee, and commend the bill to the committee of the whole house here on the basis of its study and approval by the committee on banking and commerce.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
When we were studying the principle of the proposed amendments on second reading of this bill, we of the Liberal party admitted being ready to accept amendments which would either clarify, ameliorate or render the act easier of application, but

having always in mind the welfare of the mass of the people, the consumers, without imposing too much restraint on the manufacturer. We express our doubts as to the fulfilment of this aim by the present bill. Many from the other side thought we were biased, that we were too politically minded.
The bill was passed, as we expected, and sent to the committee on banking and commerce. We heard there witnesses and briefs from all walks of life, consumers, industrialists, economists, lawyers and so forth, and we were struck or amazed in the committee by the opposition in one way or another of everyone who came before the committee.
I should like to look a little at the opposition which was shown in the committee stage by those appearing before us. First may I look at the special appendix to the proceedings, which relates to some correspondence. I do not intend to read everything that was said, but will refer to portions here and there to prove that most of those who appeared were opposed in one way or another to the proposed amendments. I should like to refer first to a letter written to the chairman of the committee by Mr. G. E. Britnell of the department of economics and political science, University of Saskatchewan. The letter is found on page 15 of the appendix to the proceedings of the standing committee, and reads as follows:
Under a covering letter to the Minister of Justice dated November 30, 1959, the senior members of the department of economics and political science at the University of Saskatchewan, professors G. E. Britnell, V. C. Fowke, N. M. Ward, K. A. H. Buckley and A. E. Safarian, submitted a criticism of Bill C-59. We regret that because of the late date on which Bill C-58 has been introduced, and the pressure of other commitments, we are now unable to submit a full appraisal of Bill C-58 for consideration by your committee.
It is the view of those who signed our original submission, however, that the amended bill carries over, in substantially unchanged form, several provisions of the original bill which were subject to serious criticism. Thus, although the wording has been changed somewhat, the amendments to section 32, listing permissible forms of co-operation between companies, are still subject to the dangers which we indicated in our submission. Furthermore, the amended bill is still likely to result in a significant weakening of the ban on resale price maintenance. Finally, our concluding suggestion that the application of the legislation to the service industries be examined has been completely ignored.
On page 27 of the same appendix there is a letter from Mr. J. H. Northway, president of the Canadian retail federation. I will not read the whole letter because I do not want to take the time of the committee by reading things which are accepted by all. However, in subparagraph 2 he says:
The penalties involved in section 33B are serious and there is a strong fear that they would provide to manufacturers an excuse to eliminate, in effect,
Combines Investigation Act
advertising allowances to retailers of all sizes. This could involve an effective prohibition of advertising allowances generally, which we think to be unfair and unrealistic.
Subparagraph 3 reads as follows:
It has been pointed out to us that the three definitions of "proportionate terms" in subsection 3 of section 33B do not stand alone but are cumulative. Therefore, in order to qualify to receive an allowance, the three definitions of "proportionate terms" must be met in the light of their total effect. It has been urged upon us that this is a practical impossibility for retailers generally, large or small, and amounts to a virtual prohibition of the receipt of advertising allowances. Advertising allowances cannot possibly be used in the same way by a small retailer as by a department store or as by a mail order house; yet the legislation presumes that this is possible.
A number of our member companies have told us that, after consulting with their solicitors, they have failed to obtain a satisfactory interpretation of the language of section 33B which would direct them as to what course of action they must follow should this section become law. It would appear that it is not possible for a retailer to know what course of action he should follow or under what circumstances he may properly receive an allowance from the manufacturing supplier.
I have referred to only two letters in the appendix, but most of them put forward criticisms of one kind or another. Therefore I want to say to the committee that even though the minister says the bill is a clarification, it would appear that most of the people who appeared before the committee do not seem to think so.
I should like to refer now to volume No. 2 of the proceedings of the committee, page 98. There we have the evidence given by Miss Atkinson, president of the national association of Canadian consumers. At page 99 I find the following:
Our opposition to resale price maintenance has been repeatedly stated and reaffirmed, not only to the various departments and committees which have considered this matter before, but it has been reaffirmed by our members at local and provincial levels and during discussions at meetings of the national delegate body. We felt that we definitely have a mandate from our consumer members to appear before you and present this case for them.
We feel that the enactment of the proposed amendment to clause 34 will seriously weaken this safeguard to consumers and make successful prosecution difficult and unlikely.
Mr. Gilbert's presentation of the distributors' case appears to pass on the desire to prevent that form of competition which he referred to as loss leader selling.
Our members and other consumers have never complained of the so-called loss leader selling. They do complain of the continuing of the price maintenance afforded by their wide use of lists and suggested prices.
Later on the same page Miss Atkinson says:
This submission will be limited very largely to a consideration of clause 14 of Bill C-58, which amends section 34 of the Combines Investigation Act prohibiting the practice of resale price maintenance. The reason for this limitation is not that

Combines Investigation Act
we necessarily approve of the remaining amendments but rather that many of them involve technical issues relating to the jurisprudence in combines cases and complex economic considerations which require a degree of specialist knowledge that is beyond our competence and our limited budget.
As found on page 100 she goes on to say:
Turning now to the amendments to section 34. it appears, on the surface, that the ban on resale price maintenance is not being eliminated but rather certain pricing, servicing and advertising practices are being brought under a limited control. Closer examination, however, makes it clear that successful prosecutions against "dealers" who enforce resale price maintenance will be most unlikely if these amendments are adopted.
Under proposed subsection (a) "no inference unfavourable to the person charged" with attempting to enforce resale price maintenance shall be drawn if "he and any one upon whose report he depended had reasonable cause to believe and did believe" that the seller made a practice of using the articles supplied as "loss leaders".
"Loss leader" selling of a product is defined as being "not for the purpose of making a profit thereon but for purposes of advertising". But at what level is it considered that a profit is being made? And why should the seller be forced to make a profit on the item in question rather than on his stock as a whole; and of course, who decides what the profit is? These are surely basic questions and the only answers that seem at all likely are very disturbing to our members.
As was suggested a little later, special discounts for advertising credits may be given to one and not to another. This would constitute quite an injustice, and we know quite well that these credits are generally given to those who are strong enough to be able to force the manufacturers to give them. They are always given to the powerful ones, but never to the small ones who may benefit from such a thing.
Later on in the minutes of evidence, No. 3, we have a brief presented by the Canadian [DOT]electrical manufacturers association. In general they seem to like some parts of the bill, and they seem to be quite critical of others. I read from page 165:
Section 29-Reduction or removal of customs duties
(section 11)
Therefore, we suggest that the words "from or as a result of an inquiry under the provisions of this act, or" in the first and second lines of the section, should be deleted.
They do not ask us to abandon this section, they just plainly ask that these words be deleted. Then in speaking of section 31 (2) -prohibition order without conviction-this is what they have to say:
Our recommendation therefore is that the underlined words "has done" be deleted in the subsection.
On page 166 we find this:
Section 32 (3)-Exceptions to the defences contained in section 32
(section 13)

The section as now written would appear to prevent even reasonable acquisitions of this kind. Section 33-Mergers and monopolies (section 13)
Bill C-59 of 1959 contained the following words:- "Subsection (1) shall not be construed or applied so as to limit or impair any right or interest derived under the Patent Act, or under any other act of the parliament of Canada." We believe these words should be added to this section to make it clear that section 33 is not intending to impair in any way rights derived from patents.
Section 33A (b) and (c)- Illegal trade practices (section 13)
Speaking of the words "solely" they said:
.. ."It is not clear what the addition of this word accomplishes but it can only have a meaning which pre-judges some future situation which may or may not arise. We think it unfortunate for the hapless trader who happens to be caught in the words of this paragraph that his fate may be determined by an opinion as to circumstances which may never arise. Mr. Chairman, in resuming my remarks at this stage perhaps it would be well to reiterate the fact that this particular bill and anti-combines legislation of this nature have a two-fold general effect or approach, one of which is to ensure that competition exists and develops, and the other to see that the consuming public is protected, as it were, to the fullest possible extent against encroachments on their rights by large industrial organizations.
When we think in terms of competition and what it means, I think we all realize that it is not an absolute term; that there are different concepts, interpretations and theories and different qualifying phrases about competition ranging from the so-called perfect competition, which is something in theory only and a basis from which to start explaining other concepts of competition, to the so-called new competition theory which generally speaking is that there is only so much money in circulation; that the consuming public has only a certain amount of money to spend on certain types of goods and, therefore, the competition is competition for the sales dollar as between firms producing different types of commodities. The

thought flowing from this concept is that it is permissible, therefore, for firms producing the same types of commodities to enter into price-setting agreements because what they are doing is not competing with each other but competing in a price sense for a portion of the consuming dollar.
I do not wish to get involved in these theoretical concepts of competition, although we do know that there are elements in the business world which promote and have promoted from time to time the development of these different concepts of what competition should mean, and which would like to argue that whatever they do within this field is permissible even though it may be that they are engaged in price fixing.
However, the benefits which flow from the competitive forces, the ones which we should concern ourselves with in so far as the general public is concerned, are twofold. One relates to a better quality product and the other relates to a lower price for any particular product or commodity.
As I said earlier, there are generally two elements which have a stake, a direct interest, in this legislation. One is industry and the other is the public. While there may be interests different from those, I think we can confine ourselves to one or the other, industry or the public. We know that industry is organized, is vocal and is divided, of course, into provincial groups, local groups and different organizations, and is able to present its points of view with much more clarity, much more expressiveness, much more effectiveness than is the consuming public. The very fact that a corporation does exist in industry is an indication that it has organized within itself.
Then we have the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, which is the voice in one field of industry. We have the various provincial sections of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the boards of trade, the chambers of commerce, which to a great degree are reflecting industry's desires and the attitudes of individual trade associations, some of which appeared before the committee. 1 refer to the fisheries association, the metal mining association and the electrical manufacturers association. There are hosts of other types of associations organized on a trade or specific industry type of basis.
These associations, as I said before, are organized; they are vocal, and they are able to present their point of view with much more effect and force than the general public, which generally speaking is unorganized in terms of an organization which relates to a matter such as this and generally speaking is not amenable to organization along these
Combines Investigation Act lines. We do have the Canadian association of consumers, which is one organization representing the consuming public, but even that organization in itself is not as effectively organized or as vocal as, for argument's sake, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association or the various trade associations to which I made reference.
It does not always follow, in fact I submit it is relatively seldom, that the specific interests of industry and of the consuming public coincide with one another. I think if one will review the various representations made to the minister, the Prime Minister and other members of the cabinet, especially those made since the introduction of bill C-59 last year, one will find that the views expressed, as I indicated earlier, by the organizations or associations representing industry had much more impact than any representations which might have been made on behalf of the general public. The effect of those representations is shown in the legislation we have before us, and was also indicated in the legislation introduced and withdrawn last year.
I think we can pretty well determine therefore that the corporate element in the industrial field, the element with a specific axe to grind, has had its views and desires reflected in this legislation more than the views of the consuming public. I submit that primarily this is because the industry groups are far more vocal and effective and are better organized and better able to present their point of view over a longer period of time than the general public. The result of the activities of these pressure groups is shown in practically every proposed change of any major importance in the legislation.
We must remember that there are a number of changes in the legislation which are necessary because of major changes in policy approach. However, every other change with the exception of two pretty well reflects the attitude of the business world as opposed to the attitude of the consuming public. The first exception is the misleading advertising section, and the second is the reference to restraining or dissolution orders without the necessity of first obtaining a conviction. Even in the case of the second one, some doubt was expressed by an eminent authority on law, the acting dean of the faculty of law of McGill University, Professor Cohen, as to the constitutionality of being able to obtain a restraining or dissolution order without first obtaining a conviction.
We know that Professor Cohen was rather verbose when he appeared before the committee, and perhaps used more words than were necessary to get his point of view across. I do not intend, therefore, to read Professor

Combines Investigation Act Cohen's evidence. I will simply say that his expression of doubt as to the constitutionality of the restraining or dissolution order provision is found on page 547 of the minutes and proceedings of evidence No. 9. If 1 were to read Professor Cohen's full remarks it would take too much of the time of the committee, so I simply give that reference in case hon. members wish to look at what he said. His remarks start a little more than two thirds of the way down page 547.
Apart from this matter, which is really only a side issue, I think I can say without too much fear of contradiction that in introducing these amendments the government has knuckled under, as it were, to specific vested interests and has not given the full consideration that it should have given to the effect of these amendments on the general consuming public. We all realize that one of the intentions of the legislation is to protect the consumer as much as possible against encroachment upon his rights, liberties and freedoms by large mass industrial organizations.
The hon. member for Ottawa West moved a motion for information listing the various representations made to the minister. I do not wish to go into them in detail at this time because my time is running short. I will merely say that a review of these representations indicates that organization after organization in the industrial world made its views known to the minister not only on this occasion but in years past. These views are reflected in the legislation before us, and the views, desires and hopes of the general consuming public have been by-passed to a great extent or glossed over or forgotten. Mr. Chairman, my remarks will be very brief. I wish to indicate that the bill before us is a very important step forward. About two years ago I came across an important problem which at that time did not seem to be covered by the Combines Investigation Act. It had to do with abuses on the part of one or two major oil companies which, in order to get volume, made highly secret and most unorthodox deals with the larger users whereby prices would be drastically cut and the oil companies would get the volume they needed. At the same time the small consumer purchasing oil to heat his house or the small industrial plant owner using oil or oil products to heat or operate his factory got no such benefit. At that time I felt that the large consumers were getting a very unfair advantage at the expense of


the smaller consumers. However, the government could do very little then by way of an inquiry, and I am pleased to see that this bill will make possible inquiries into that practice.
In a riding such as mine we have a very difficult problem with regard to the prices being paid for pulpwood. I realize that investigation and prosecution with respect to the price fixing of pulpwood have almost been terminated. However, I should like to say that the new section 13, which gives the minister the right to appoint counsel to assist the investigation will probably also give more control to the minister through the department's counsel in order to bring some influence to bear on the methods used in carrying out these investigations. From information that has been made public at various times I can say that the investigation conducted with regard to the price of pulpwood did not reflect any credit on the government which conducted it. Methods of getting information were adopted in the offices of these pulp and paper companies which were highly unethical, undemocratic and without proper regard for due process of law and the other constitutional safeguards which our citizens have a right to expect.
Naturally, there is no question but that action has to be taken in regard to the price of pulpwood. I know that in my riding the price of pulpwood has gone down from $6 a cord two years ago to $4 per cord. This has occurred at a time when the cost of living is increasing and when wages in the pulp mills have reached the highest levels they have ever attained. The price of pulpwood has gone down by some 30 per cent in some cases.
I do not relate this, however, to any combination of factors amongst the pulp and paper companies; I do not say that is the primary cause of this reduction in price. However, I do say that the people who have to earn their living by cutting pulpwood are being placed in a very unfair position. In most cases, because of the large expanse of territory in which they work and because of the difficulty in getting them together to form a union, these people are denied the benefits that employees in the pulp mills have had guaranteed to them by the efforts of their unions. Is it fair, for instance, that a man who sweeps the floor in the pulp mill should receive $1.70 per hour, while the fellow who cuts pulpwood from morning until night should make only $4 or $5 a day. At the end of the week, when he has paid for his horse and other living expenses in camp, he may find himself left with only $15, whereas the fellow in the pulp mill may take home $75.

I feel that if there has been some definite combination of circumstances which has been fostered by the pulp and paper companies- and I have no reason to think there has- whereby the price of pulpwood is being forced down, then some definite action should be taken. If our people are being forced to eke out a living on wages which are 30 per cent less than they were, I certainly feel that this act, as it will be applied, should go a long way toward offsetting the detrimental effects of the reduction in the price of pulp-wood. Of course I realize that, fundamentally, the people who are engaged in the cutting of pulpwood are not unionized; they are not united. I know that a few years ago some efforts were made-as a matter of fact I took part in them-to organize the woodsmen of northern New Brunswick into a union. This effort did have some beneficial results and conditions in the camps improved. However, the fact still remains-

We heard from a good many of the witnesses that the loss leader practice is leading to a great deal of difficulty for the small businessman in this country. We feel that the small businessman is the backbone of the economy and if he is forced out of business this trade will be taken over by the larger concern, the chain store. Combines Investigation Act he means that then they would be able to deal with investigations of this sort in an easier and quicker manner than possible under the act at the moment; yet I cannot for the life of me-I hope the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska will clear this point up-see how that is possible. I say that because the minister himself said that there are no substantial changes in the legislation, only changes designed for clarification purposes. There was nothing to do with additional research facilities, or with additional investigatory powers given to the officials of the branch, or with additional staff; it is merely the same act only clarified.
I think the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska does not have a correct understanding of the bill. Certainly if his understanding is correct, I for one would appreciate it very much if he was able to direct my attention to the clauses of the bill which he thinks give added powers of investigation, and so forth, because I have not yet been able to find any.
I would also like to make one other comment which deals with the references in the bill to the application of section 32 and the amendments thereto. That is the section dealing with combinations, agreements and conspiracies which are in restraint of trade, enhanced prices, and things of that nature. Some presentations were made before the banking and commerce committee to the effect that perhaps these amendments are a subtle way of bringing in the so-called specific detriment aspect which courts have refused to consider up to now. The courts have taken the view, and the witnesses appearing before the committee also took the view, that the courts should not be called on to assess any specific detriment to the public of any agreement or conspiracy which the parties charged may have entered into. The courts and the economists take the position that this is a task too difficult for the courts to deal with, and that if we are to bring before the courts such cases and insist that the courts make an assessment as to the specific detriment caused by any such conspiracy, and so on, the courts would be doing nothing else than listening to arguments of opposing counsel about theoretical concepts of economics or competition and it would be almost impossible to assess what the specific detriment was.
Dr. Skeoch, who is now professor of economics at Queen's University and for some years was senior economist in the combines investigation branch, had some thoughts in this regard which I think will be of interest. He was senior economist to the combines investigation branch of the Department of

Justice for about seven years, and prior to that was senior economist with the Canadian wheat board. Dr. Skeoch made a reference to this specific detriment question on page 432 of the minutes of proceedings, where the brief which he read was reproduced, and he said as follows:
To suggest, as the brief of the Canadian metal mining association on Bill C-59 did, that our courts are capable of determining the effects of interferences with competition because they "deal with complex subjects, such as those relating to income tax, customs and patents, and weigh technical evidence submitted to them by specialists and experts" is to fail to understand the nature of the issues under consideration. The courts are not required to assess the incidence of the income tax, to determine its effect on the level of savings and investment and the like, all of which would be involved in determining the effects of the income tax. Nor are they required to determine whether our patent laws promote or hinder innovation and development, either in general or in a specific case.
It might be added that if parliament were to enact legislation requiring the courts to forecast the trend of stock market prices, the hilarious reception such an enactment would receive can easily be imagined. Yet to determine the specific effects of combines restricting competition would be a far more complex matter.
This is not quite so clear a reflection of the government's attitude in this regard as was Bill No. C-59 of last year. If I may be allowed to make one or two references to that bill, I submit it indicates government attitude, but much has since been covered in the bill before us. On page 4 of Bill No. C-59, the proposed new section 19 (l)(a) with respect to the restrictive trades commission reads as follows:
(a)	where it appears that a conspiracy, combination, agreement or arrangement has existed, shall include a finding whether or not the conspiracy, combination, agreement or arrangement relates in whole or in part to any of the matters specified in subparagraphs (i) to (v) of paragraph (a) of subsection (2) of section 32 and, if not, shall include a finding whether or not the conspiracy, combination, agreement or arrangement, in the opinion of the commission, has operated, or is likely in the foreseeable future to operate to the specific and substantial detriment of the public-
Et cetera.

In a prosecution for an offence under subsection
(1), it is a defence if the accused ...
(b)	also establishes that the conspiracy, combination, agreement or arrangement has not operated and is not likely to operate to the specific detriment of the public, whether consumers, producers or others.
May I point out that these references to last year's bill make express reference to the

words "specific detriment", and that while the minister says that the proposed changes to section 32 are for purposes of clarification only, a great deal of the evidence submitted to the committee, although there was some conflict, some people saying yes and others no, was directed toward injecting these specific detriment arguments into the courts which would be a serious weakening of the combines laws themselves.

May I go on with the case I have been presenting? I was quoting some of the evidence which was given by Professor Maxwell Cohen, acting dean of the faculty of law, McGill University, and I had come to the sixth point which he made during the examination of his point of view. Professor Cohen said:
My sixth point was concerned with this new section dealing with promotional allowances. You will notice the notes to your bill at page 7 indicate that this particular proposal, now section 33 (b), results from the report of the Stewart royal commission on price spreads of food products.
I have no strong feelings on this matter. It seems to me, as a practical question it may he very difficult to work out some of the technical aspects in applying clauses 3(a), (b) and (c). I will give you an example:	supposing the Admiral
radio corporation is going to give a promotional allowance to Eatons in the amount of $100,000 a year; it must give something proportionate to Mr. "X" at the corner store, say in the amount of $500 a year, in relationship to the size of his sales as compared to Eatons, to "equalize" the promotional facilities on each side. I think this is a very difficult thing to administer. Obviously, this is something of an injustice which the royal

commission felt because, yet which the actual situation, it makes the result ridiculous. For example, in the case of Eatons receiving $100,000 a year promotional allowances from the Admiral radio people and, Mr. Smith, in the comer store, in terms of his sales, is entitled to $500, that $500 does not give him much promotional opportunity and it seems somewhat absurd. So, the actual relative fairness in that bill may leave you, in the end, with a very great absolute difference between the respective capacities to promote.
With respect to his seventh point Mr. Cohen was not too critical. He said:
My seventh point is the one of misleading advertising-the new section; section 33 (c).
He goes on to say:
When you relate section 33(c) to the new proposals under 31(2), the right to get a restraining order before a conviction, we now may be in the same position as the federal trade commission is in in its "cease and desist" orders. Because the federal trade commission can issue a "cease and desist" order to a company that has been carrying on this misleading kind of advertising for years. We could not do that before; but looking at 33(c) here, in relation to restraining orders before conviction, it seems to me that we are now in this position, that we have virtually the same powers as the federal trade commission exercised, and seems to have exercised quite sensibly since 1914 in the United States.
Mr. Cohen's eighth point was as follows:
My eighth point is the loss leader problem, at the bottom of page 8, clause 14 of the amendments, section 34 of the act. I suppose, next to the new defences I mentioned with respect to loose-knit combinations a moment ago, this is the most controversial part of the bill. What puzzles me about the proposal is this. After all, we have had some major studies in Canada by the director and by the commission, which have shown over the years that though the loss leader question is dramatized heavily by some manufacturers and some associations, the actual number of instances in which you can find persons selling at less than a profit-however you define the word "profit": and it is not easy to define what is a profit- are so small as not to make it a serious problem for purposes of measurement. You cannot find enough instances to say that this is a serious problem, if one is to take the coast-to-coast surveys that were made on this subject.
Therefore, I ask myself the question: if the objective inquiries we have made, which have been made by responsible people, show that the number of cases in fact are very few, why is there this urgency to put into the bill something which opens doors to a very large number of new possible abuses?
The abuses here are twofold. First, it is going to be very difficult to administer clauses (a), (b),
(c), (d) and (e), in terms of the language itself; not only because words like "profit" are hard to define; but words like, in clause (d) on page 9, "level of servicing" are going to be very difficult to define. Words like "unfairly disparaging" are going to be very hard to administer. Not only that, but much more significant, I suggest to you, is the introduction to section 14, clause (5), because if you look at page 8, at the bottom, you will notice that the language encourages a whole system of what I would like to call private informers; a whole system of basing a private regulatory mechanism upon gossip, upon subjective impressions, and not upon objective data. Look how the language now reads;

"Where, in a prosecution under this section, it is proved that the person charged refused or counselled the refusal to sell or supply an article to any other person, no inference unfavourable to the person charged shall be drawn from such evidence if he satisfies the court that he and any one upon whose report he depended. .. Not only he; but, any one upon whose report he depended."
-had reasonable cause to believe and did believe. Just think of that as a defence! Think of the number of letters that might be written to a manufacturer by an aggrieved retail competitor, by someone who is angry or annoyed because he simply is losing out and claims that disparagement is involved, and who claims that things are being sold at less than a profit. And then the vendor says, "I am going to cut you off." He cannot cut them off now, under 34.
At page 561 Mr. Cohen stated:
I come now to my last point. That is a very interesting and novel idea which comes to us, for the first time, in this country-namely that there should be an option, if all the accused agree, except in one case, to go to the Exchequer Court of Canada for these proceedings under this act...
I do not say for one moment that persons as able as the President of the Exchequer Court of Canada-who once taught me evidence, for whom I have a great fondness, are not judges of the highest rank. I am not speaking at all ad hominem. I am sure that every member of the exchequer court would approach this act with as much objectivity, fairness, detachment and skill as they would approach any other piece of legislation. I merely suggest that the atmosphere of the tribunal is an atmosphere which may affect the approach to the kind of problems before them. The atmosphere of that tribunal is partially determined by its major preoccupation, in areas where such matters as restrictions on trade are legal. It is a tribunal without the usual attributes of criminal jurisdiction. It thinks of punishment in terms of other standards, but not in terms of the criminal law and imprisonment. It is accustomed to nonimprisonment sanctions, but not imprisonment sanctions.
I could quote at great length from the remarks of Mr. Cohen who was one of the clearest witnesses to appear before the committee. I think we may discuss these matters further when we come to the specific clauses of the bill.
I turn now to the minutes and proceedings of the committee on banking and commerce, No. 10, dated July 11, 1960. The witness appearing on that occasion was Dr. H, H. Hannam, president and managing director of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. He presented the view of the farmer as a producer, a consumer and a businessman. He suggested that the farmer has a special stake in the combines legislation and that he is required to be an expert as a producer and as a distributor as well.
With respect to clause 14 of the bill, the clause relating to the resale price maintenance, he stated:
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture has consistently supported the principles of public policy embodied in section 34 of the present Combines Investigation Act. It is this section which makes it an offence for a dealer to set up his own

This is what Mr. Hannam had to say at page 592:
Let us look at these five practices which provide defences for refusal to supply:
(1)	The use of an article as a loss leader for purposes of advertising, not for the purpose of making a profit on the article. In our opinion this provision clearly opens the way to the establishment of resale price maintenance.
(2)	The sale of articles not for the purpose of selling such articles at a profit but for the purpose of attracting customers to the store in the hope of selling them other articles. This provision in the amendments is in many ways similar in nature and intent to the previous one regarding loss leaders. Our objections to it are the same-that this should not be a matter for private determination; that it is extremely imprecise for purposes of legal interpretation, and that it will open up a road to resale price maintenance.
(3)	Engaging in misleading advertising in respect to an article. We do not support misleading advertising, and believe that it should be a matter for continuous review and policing by public authority. If it can be proved by an official investigation that a retailer is engaging in misleading advertising, then prosecution should follow. But again, we believe that to place the policing of this matter in the hands of dealers can only open up another avenue to the achievement of what we are trying to avoid, that is, resale price maintenance.
(4)	Inadequate levels of servicing for the purchasers of articles. We firmly believe that to permit the re-establishment of resale price maintenance because in the opinion of a manufacturer or other supplier his products are being inadequately serviced by a retailer or other seller, could result in the complete elimination of the existing prohibition on resale price maintenance, which prohibition has contributed so much to the freeing of price competition for countless commodities now marketed in Canada.
(5)	Unfairly disparaging the value of articles supplied, in relation to their price or otherwise. This question of disparagement is, in our opinion, perhaps the most unsatisfactory of all... We would be inclined to think that any dealer desirous of enforcing resale price maintenance for his product would consider that any selling of that product below his suggested price, would constitute disparaging the value of the article in relation to its price.
It is quite clear that the representatives of the farmers do not seem to agree very much with the idea put forward by the Minister of Justice. Farther on, Mr. Hannam had this to say:
In conclusion: the farmers of Canada will be disappointed if parliament passes a bill whose effect proves to be the weakening of price competition between their suppliers-which is bound to aggravate further the unfair relationship now existing between the price levels at which the farmer sells and buys.
I should have liked to read more of the evidence given, Mr. Chairman, but I pass over a lot of it. It would have proved more clearly that our point of view expressed on second reading of the bill, when we spoke on the principle, is the real point of view of the

Most of those who are in favour of the bill, if they had attended the committee sessions, would have seen that those who favoured a small part of the bill were against the main parts of the bill. Those representing the important part of our society, namely the consumers, were far from being in accord with the minister. They claim it would be unfair if we took away the prohibition against price maintenance; it would be unfair to the small businessman if we wanted to retain him in business. We know that all of the failures and bankruptcies are not in the field of the small businessman. We have had more failures and bankruptcies this year among contractors in the building industry, and this cannot be on account of the prohibition against retail price maintenance.
